As commander of the [Continental Army](/wiki/Continental_Army "Continental Army"), Washington led [Patriot](/wiki/Patriot_(American_Revolution) "Patriot (American Revolution)") forces to victory in the [American Revolutionary War](/wiki/American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War") against the [British Empire](/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire"). He is commonly known as the [Father of His Country](/wiki/Father_of_the_Nation "Father of the Nation") for his role in bringing about [American independence](/wiki/American_independence "American independence").

Born in the [Colony of Virginia](/wiki/Colony_of_Virginia "Colony of Virginia"), Washington became the commander of the [Virginia Regiment](/wiki/Virginia_Regiment "Virginia Regiment") during the [French and Indian War](/wiki/French_and_Indian_War "French and Indian War") (1754–1763). He was later elected to the Virginia [House of Burgesses](/wiki/House_of_Burgesses "House of Burgesses"), and opposed the perceived oppression of the American colonists by the British Crown. When the American Revolutionary War against the British began in 1775, Washington was appointed [commander-in-chief of the Continental Army](/wiki/Commanding_General_of_the_United_States_Army "Commanding General of the United States Army"). He directed a poorly organized and equipped force against disciplined British troops. Washington and his army achieved an early victory at the [Siege of Boston](/wiki/Siege_of_Boston "Siege of Boston") in March 1776 but were forced to [retreat from New York City](/wiki/New_York_and_New_Jersey_campaign "New York and New Jersey campaign") in November. Armand d'Armailhac of [Château d'Armailhac](/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_d%27Armailhac "Château d'Armailhac") *(bottle picture)* and Baron Hector de Brane of Château Mouton were important figures in the establishment of Cabernet Sauvignon in Bordeaux.

The [Bordeaux wine region](/wiki/Bordeaux_wine_region "Bordeaux wine region") is intimately connected with Cabernet Sauvignon, even though wine is rarely made without the blended component of other grape varieties. It is the likely place of origin of the vine, and producers across the globe have invested heavily in trying to reproduce the structure and complexity of Bordeaux wines. While the "Bordeaux blend" of Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and Merlot created the earliest examples of acclaimed Cabernet Sauvignon wine, Cabernet Sauvignon was first blended in Bordeaux with [Syrah](/wiki/Syrah "Syrah") (from the Northern Rhone), a pairing that is widely seen in Australia and some *vin de pays* wines from the [Languedoc](/wiki/Languedoc_(wine) "Languedoc (wine)").

The decision to first start blending Cabernet Sauvignon was partly derived from financial necessity. The sometimes temperamental and unpredictable climate of Bordeaux during the "[Little Ice Age](/wiki/Little_Ice_Age "Little Ice Age")" did not guarantee a successful harvest every year; producers had to insure themselves against the risk of losing an entire vintage by planting a variety of grapes. Over time it was discovered that the unique characteristics of each grape variety could complement each other and enhance the quality of the wine. Cabernet Sauvignon added structure, [acidity](/wiki/Acidity "Acidity"), tannins and aging potential as a base or backbone of the wine. He remembers his adoptive mother, Lillian Spellman Ellison,[[9]](#cite_note-:2-9) as warm and loving. He found his adoptive father, Louis Ellison, to be austere, unsupportive, and often distant. A government employee who had made a small fortune in Chicago real estate, only to lose it during the [Great Depression](/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression"), Louis had chosen his last name to honor [Ellis Island](/wiki/Ellis_Island "Ellis Island"), his point of entry into the United States.[[7]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTESymondsEllison2004332–33-7)

At the conclusion of oral argument, the case is submitted for decision. Cases are decided by majority vote of the justices. After the oral argument is concluded, usually in the same week as the case was submitted, the justices retire to another conference at which the preliminary votes are tallied and the court sees which side has prevailed. One of the justices in the majority is then assigned to write the court's opinion, also known as the "majority opinion", an assignment made by the most senior justice in the majority, with the chief justice always being considered the most senior. Drafts of the court's opinion circulate among the justices until the court is prepared to announce the judgment in a particular case.[[220]](#cite_note-220)

Justices are free to change their votes on a case up until the decision is finalized and published. In any given case, a justice is free to choose whether or not to author an opinion or else simply join the majority or another justice's opinion. There are several primary types of opinions:

* **Opinion of the court**: this is the binding decision of the Supreme Court. An opinion that more than half of the justices join (usually at least five justices, since there are nine justices in total; but in cases where some justices do not participate it could be fewer) is known as "majority opinion" and creates binding precedent in American law. Whereas an opinion that fewer than half of the justices join is known as a "plurality opinion" and is only partially binding precedent.
* **Concurring**: a justice agrees with and joins the majority opinion but authors a separate concurrence to give additional explanations, rationales, or commentary. Concurrences do not create binding precedent.
* **Concurring in the judgment**: a justice agrees with the outcome the court reached but disagrees with its reasons for doing so. A justice in this situation does not join the majority opinion. Like regular concurrences, these do not create binding precedent.
